intro.html: Some things matter more than anything; others hardly matter at all. These words help you rank what is important, from the one thing everything depends on to the side issue that can wait.

Very important: crucial (it decides the outcome), pivotal (everything turns on it), paramount (above all else), preeminent (best of all), salient (stands out; most noticeable). Not important: trivial, trifling (small), frivolous (silly), peripheral (at the edge) and tangential (off the point).

words.def: extremely important; deciding how things turn out
words.ex: Getting enough sleep is {crucial} the night before a big test.
words.ctx: The last-second catch was {crucial}: without it, the other team would have scored and won the championship.
words.etym: From Latin crux, “cross,” through the idea of a crossroads, where a traveler must choose the right way.

mn.text: At the crossroads, one sign points home and the other points to the swamp. Choosing the right road is {crucial}!

scene.alt: A boy with a backpack stops at a forest signpost, choosing between the road home and the road to the swamp.

words.def: of central importance; the point on which everything turns
words.ex: Winning the coin toss turned out to be {pivotal} in the close game.
words.ctx: Meeting her chemistry teacher was a {pivotal} moment in Ada’s life; before that, she had never thought about science, and afterward she could think of little else.
words.etym: From pivot, the pin or point on which something turns.

mn.text: The whole seesaw tips up and down on one little pin in the middle. Without it, nothing moves: the pin is {pivotal}.

scene.alt: Two children play on a seesaw, with its middle pin, the pivot, circled.

words.ex: On the field trip, safety was {paramount}.
words.ctx: For the rescue team, speed was {paramount}; every minute counted, so they left their lunches behind and ran.
words.etym: From Anglo-French paramont, “above, at the top,” going back to Latin ad montem, “to the mountain.”

mn.cue: PARA-MOUNT: high above the rest, like a MOUNTain
mn.text: On Tia’s hiking list, “Stay safe” towers above everything else, like a mountain over little hills. Safety is {paramount}.

scene.alt: A hiker points to a huge rock labeled Safety that towers over small rocks labeled snacks and speed.

words.def: better or more famous than all others in a field
words.ex: She is the {preeminent} expert on spiders in the whole country.
words.ctx: Many bakers in the city made good bread, but Nell’s shop was {preeminent}: people crossed town and waited an hour in line just to buy her sourdough.
words.etym: From Latin praeeminere, “to stand out above”: prae (before, above) + eminere (to stand out).

mn.cue: PRE-EMINENT: stands out above even the famous
mn.text: There are many famous bakers in town, but Nell stands out above them all; her line stretches around the block. She is {preeminent}.

scene.alt: A baker wearing a medal hands out bread to a long line of happy customers.

words.def: most noticeable or important; standing out
words.ex: The {salient} feature of the old house was its bright red door.
words.ctx: The report was long, but Sami picked out its {salient} points: the bridge was unsafe, repairs would cost a million dollars, and work had to start before winter.
words.etym: From Latin salire, “to leap”: a salient point leaps out at you.
words.note: Salient means standing out, not salty.

mn.cue: SAIL-ient: the one red SAILboat that LEAPS out
mn.text: Among all the white sailboats on the bay, one is bright red. It leaps out at you: the red boat is the {salient} sight.

scene.alt: A boy points at the one red-sailed boat among many white ones.

words.ex: Don’t worry about such a {trivial} mistake; it was only one comma.
words.ctx: To Dev, the scratch on his bike seemed {trivial} next to the real problem: the front wheel was bent and would not turn at all.
words.etym: From Latin trivialis, “commonplace,” from trivium, “a place where three roads meet.”

mn.cue: TRIVIA-l: a tiny fact that hardly matters
mn.text: Zoe frets that her left sock is one shade darker than her right. It’s a {trivial} difference; no one will ever notice.

scene.alt: A worried girl studies two almost identical socks with a magnifying glass while her cat looks bored.

words.ex: The repair cost a {trifling} sum: just two dollars for a new screw.
words.ctx: Compared with the flood that soaked the whole basement, the dripping faucet was a {trifling} problem, so Dad decided it could wait until spring.

mn.text: The ring toss costs one penny, and Ivy flips it into the jar without a second thought: a {trifling} sum.

scene.alt: A girl flips a single penny into a jar at a shop counter.

words.def: not serious; silly or not worth taking seriously
words.ex: Grandpa thought buying a hat for the dog was {frivolous}, but the dog loved it.
words.ctx: With only twenty dollars left for groceries, Mom said that spending ten on balloons would be {frivolous}, so we drew decorations instead.

mn.text: Victor buys his cat a tiny jeweled crown and a velvet throne. Frilly, silly and not needed at all: the purchases are {frivolous}.

scene.alt: A man bows to his cat, who sits on a velvet throne wearing a tiny crown.

words.def: at the edge; of minor importance
words.ex: The new bus line will reach even the {peripheral} neighborhoods at the edge of town.
words.ctx: The main question was how to pay for the new library; the color of its carpet was a {peripheral} issue that could wait until later.
words.etym: From Greek periphereia, “the line around a circle”: peri (around) + pherein (to carry).

mn.text: The soccer game rages in the middle of the field, but little Theo is out at the edge picking daisies. His part in the game is {peripheral}.

scene.alt: Two players race for the ball in the middle of the field while a toddler picks flowers at the edge.

words.def: only slightly connected to the main point; going off the topic
words.ex: The speaker’s {tangential} story about his cat had nothing to do with the budget.
words.ctx: Asked about his science project, Kai gave a {tangential} answer: he started with the volcano model but soon wandered off into a story about his summer vacation.
words.etym: From tangent, a line that touches a circle at one point and then goes off on its own, from Latin tangere, “to touch.”
words.note: A tangential remark touches the topic and then heads off in another direction; to go off on a tangent is to wander from the subject.

mn.cue: TANGENT: touches the topic, then shoots OFF
mn.text: Professor Edwin starts the history lesson, then shoots off: “…which reminds me of my cat, who once…” His story is {tangential}.

scene.alt: An old professor wanders off the subject into a story about his cat while two students look puzzled and bored.

after.cap: From what matters most to what hardly matters.

after.html: Salient means standing out, not salty: it comes from Latin salire, to leap, so a salient point leaps out at you. And a tangential remark is like a tangent line in geometry: it touches the topic at one point and then heads off on its own.

opts.s: When a storm is coming, getting every boat into the harbor is {paramount}; nothing else matters until they are safe.
opts.why: Something that matters more than anything else is paramount.

items.why: False. Salient means standing out or most noticeable, from Latin salire, to leap.

items.q: Asked about the history test, Dev talked about his dog’s birthday party. His answer was…
items.why: An answer that wanders off the main point is tangential.
Peri- means around, as in perimeter: peripheral things lie around the edge.

items.q: Which word is the opposite of crucial?
items.why: Crucial means extremely important; trivial means of little importance.

items.q: Type the adjective for something silly and not worth taking seriously.
items.why: Frivolous comes from Latin frivolus, silly or worthless.
